title: How to run a fair raffle with one slip of paper
description:
You don't know how many guests are coming, and you only have one slip of paper. Write the first guest's name; when guest number k arrives, they take the slip with a 1 in k chance (a coin for guest 2, a die showing 1 or 2 for guest 3). Guest one survives each swap with chance 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, ... and the product cancels to exactly 1 in 100 after 100 guests, the same as every other guest. Computers use the same trick, reservoir sampling (Algorithm R, Waterman; published by Vitter in 1985), to pick fair samples from data streams of unknown length.

Numbers checked in code: the exact fractions for all 100 guests and 200,000 simulated parties. Source: Wikipedia, Reservoir sampling.

facts_checked: Guest k takes the slip with chance 1/k: coin 1/2, die 1-2 = 1/3, guest 10 = 1/10; guest one survives 1/2 x 2/3 x 3/4 x ... x 99/100 = 1/100; exact chance for each of 100 guests = 1/100; 200,000 simulated parties: every guest 0.95%-1.06% (verify.py)

Algorithm R: item i replaces the stored item with probability given by a uniform index in 1..i; one pass over a population of unknown size; discovered by Alan G. Waterman, cited via Knuth and Vitter, 'Random sampling with a reservoir' (1985) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reservoir_sampling)

beats.say: Keep every name, or keep just one. Both pick a fair winner.
Your party raffle. Guests keep arriving, you don't know how many, and you have one slip of paper.
Give it to the first guest? Unfair. The last? Also unfair.
Guest one arrives. Write their name on the slip.
Guest two: flip a coin. Heads, they take the slip.
Guest three: roll a die. One or two, that's one in three, and it's theirs. Guest 10 gets one in 10.
But guest one has to survive every swap. Aren't they doomed?
They survive guest two half the time, then two in three, then three in four. Multiply, and everything cancels.
After 100 guests, guest one has exactly one in 100. So does everyone. And you never needed to know the count.
Computers pick samples from endless data the same way. It's called reservoir sampling.
